prompt: A Cassandra node is down for 14 days, while a large batch of rows is deleted. `gc_grace_seconds` is the default 10 days, and the node is brought back without running repair first. What is the risk?

options.text: Deleted data can reappear if other replicas have purged their tombstones and the stale node returns without a safe recovery procedure
options.explanation: If deletion tombstones have been safely purged on the other replicas before the stale node returns, old values can reappear. Purge is not automatic exactly at 10 days. Complete repair before grace expires and follow safe replacement/rebuild procedures for an overdue node.

options.text: None. Hinted handoff will deliver all the deletes
options.explanation: Wrong. Hints are only kept for a limited window (3 hours by default in Cassandra), so after 14 days most of the deletes weren't hinted.

options.text: The node will refuse to start
options.explanation: Do not rely on startup alone to prove stale data is safe. Follow the deployed version’s downtime and replacement safeguards; exact startup behaviour depends on configuration.

options.text: Reads become slower due to extra tombstones, but data stays correct
options.explanation: Wrong. If deletion markers were purged while this node retained old values, correctness is at risk, not merely read performance.

workedExample: A replica misses a deletion. Other replicas may later purge the tombstone once grace and compaction conditions allow it. If the old value then returns without the deletion marker, repair can resurrect it. Complete repair within the required grace period and use a safe recovery/replacement procedure for overdue replicas; do not assume a periodic command invocation proves repair completion.

prompt: You store IoT sensor readings in Cassandra. Rows are written once, never updated, read mostly for the last 24 hours, and expire after 30 days via TTL. Which compaction strategy fits best?

options.explanation: Not the best fit. STCS mixes old and new data into ever-larger SSTables, so expired rows linger inside big files that only compact rarely. It wastes disk and needs lots of headroom.
LCS can improve point-read file overlap, but repeatedly rewriting immutable expiring data may be a poor trade-off here. TWCS can group similarly aged data for safe whole-file expiry.

TWCS is a good candidate for mostly immutable, consistently expiring time-series data. Entire SSTables can be dropped only when fully expired and safe under tombstone/overlap rules; file count and read cost are not fixed.
Wrong. Without compaction, SSTable count grows without limit, read amplification explodes and expired data is never removed.

workedExample: One-day TWCS windows group similarly aged immutable data, which can make whole-file expiry efficient. The active window can contain multiple SSTables; closed-window file counts and query fan-out depend on compaction state, partitions and late data. TTL expiry alone does not imply immediate deletion on day 31: grace and overlap safety checks still apply. Mixed TTLs and late writes can delay reclamation.

prompt: Which statements about keeping replicas in sync in a Dynamo-style store are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With a sloppy quorum, exceeding the home-replica count with read and write counts does not guarantee intersection: write acknowledgements can come from stand-in nodes.
options.explanation: Correct. That's the trade-off of sloppy quorums. They improve write availability during failures, at the cost of the overlap guarantee until hints are handed off.

options.text: Merkle trees skip matching subtrees and localize differing key ranges, often reducing comparison traffic substantially.
options.explanation: For an ideal balanced tree with one key per leaf, sparse differences can be localised with roughly O(k × log N) hash comparisons, where k is the number of differing keys, N the number of keys, and O(...) means "grows in proportion to". Cassandra uses range trees: differing leaves can require streaming more data than the changed keys, and building trees scans data.

options.text: Read repair alone guarantees all replicas eventually converge
options.explanation: Wrong. Read repair only fixes keys that are *read*. Cold keys that are never read can stay divergent for ever, which is why periodic anti-entropy (Merkle) repair is still needed.

options.text: Hinted handoff covers short outages: a stand-in stores writes for a down replica and delivers them when it returns
options.explanation: Correct. Hints bridge transient failures. They're bounded in time (Cassandra's default hint window is 3 hours), beyond which repair has to take over.

options.text: Gossip guarantees every node learns of a failure within exactly one second
options.explanation: Wrong. Gossip spreads information probabilistically in O(log N) rounds, where N is the number of nodes: the rounds grow with the logarithm of the cluster size. Failure detection (for example phi accrual) is a suspicion level, not a deterministic deadline.

workedExample: Sloppy placement can acknowledge a write on a stand-in outside the later read’s home set, so the fixed-set intersection argument no longer applies. Hints cover recorded short outages. Merkle comparison skips matching represented ranges, but building trees and streaming differing ranges still costs I/O. Cold keys may never receive read repair, so periodic repair remains necessary.
